## In 60 seconds

An electrophysiology (EP) study records electrograms from a few catheters inside the heart and paces from them. A
catheter at the His bundle splits atrioventricular (AV) conduction into the **AH** interval, through the AV node, and
the **HV** interval, through the His–Purkinje system. Pacing protocols probe the tissue: **premature beats** after a
train (S1–S2) trace recovery curves and find refractory periods; **incremental pacing** shortens the cycle length until
conduction fails, and the AV node fails gradually, lengthening its conduction time beat by beat until a beat blocks
(**Wenckebach** periodicity). During a reentrant tachycardia, pacing slightly faster than the tachycardia captures the
circuit without stopping it: **entrainment**. When pacing stops, the time to the next local beat, the **post-pacing
interval** (PPI), tells how far the pacing site is from the circuit. These measurements are what a mapping system
annotates, and they are simple enough to model.

## From the field

- **The His recording started it.** Scherlag and colleagues described a catheter technique for recording His-bundle
  activity in man [@scherlag1969], the basis of AH and HV measurement.
- **The AV node slows before it blocks.** In rabbit preparations the anterograde nodal conduction time ranged from a
  minimum of 57 ± 2 ms to a maximum of 150 ± 13 ms, with a nodal effective refractory period of 91 ± 10 ms
  [@reid2003]. With these values, a recovery-curve model gives 1:1 conduction down to 241 ms, then 4:3 at 220 ms and
  2:1 at 150 ms (lab part C).
- **Entrainment finds circuit sites.** After myocardial infarction, radiofrequency current terminated ventricular
  tachycardia more often where the post-pacing interval approximated the tachycardia cycle length (odds ratio 4.6) or
  entrainment showed concealed fusion (odds ratio 3.4) [@stevenson1993].
- **Not every site with concealed fusion is in the circuit.** In the same study, PPI and stimulus-to-QRS analysis
  suggested that 25% of sites with concealed fusion were bystanders [@stevenson1993].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $t_A$, $t_H$, $t_V$ local activation times of the atrial, His and ventricular deflections
(ms); AH, HV intervals (ms). NCT nodal conduction time; RT recovery time since the node last conducted; $\text{ERP}_N$
nodal effective refractory period; $\text{NCT}_{\min}$, $\text{NCT}_{\max}$ its limits; $\tau$ recovery time constant;
CL pacing cycle length (ms). TCL tachycardia cycle length; PPI post-pacing interval (ms); $d$ distance from the pacing
site to the circuit (mm); CV conduction velocity along that path (mm/ms = m/s).

### Intervals

A catheter at the His bundle records three deflections each beat: atrial, His and ventricular. With local activation
times taken at the steepest downslope of each (m22):

$$
\text{AH} = t_H - t_A, \qquad \text{HV} = t_V - t_H
$$ {#eq-m11-intervals}

AH is dominated by conduction through the AV node and HV by conduction through the His–Purkinje system, so the two
locate delay or block along the AV axis; it is the His-bundle recording [@scherlag1969] that makes the split possible. On a synthetic recording with noise, the steepest-slope
times give both intervals within 0.2 ms (lab part A). Real recordings need care with far-field signals and with a His
deflection that is small next to atrial and ventricular ones.

**Key takeaways**

- AH measures nodal conduction; HV measures His–Purkinje conduction.
- Both depend on how local activation time is defined on each deflection.

### The AV nodal recovery curve

The AV node conducts more slowly when it has had less time to recover since it last conducted. A recovery curve
describes this:

$$
\text{NCT}(\text{RT}) = \text{NCT}_{\min} + (\text{NCT}_{\max} - \text{NCT}_{\min})\,e^{-(\text{RT} - \text{ERP}_N)/\tau}, \qquad \text{RT} \ge \text{ERP}_N
$$ {#eq-m11-avnode}

Below $\text{ERP}_N$ the node blocks. Premature atrial beats after a steady train measure the curve point by point; the
longest coupling interval that blocks gives $\text{ERP}_N$. We use the rabbit anterograde values above [@reid2003] with
an illustrative $\tau$ = 100 ms. Billette's group showed that a blocked beat can still reset the node's excitability,
concealed conduction [@xu2006], which this one-variable model ignores.

### Wenckebach periodicity

With atrial pacing at a fixed cycle length, each beat's recovery time is the cycle length minus the previous beat's
nodal conduction time, $\text{RT}_n = \text{CL} - \text{NCT}_{n-1}$. A long conduction time leaves less recovery for
the next beat. The steady 1:1 state needs $\text{RT} \ge \text{ERP}_N$, so

$$
\text{CL}_W = \text{ERP}_N + \text{NCT}_{\max}, \qquad \text{stable if } \frac{\text{NCT}_{\max} - \text{NCT}_{\min}}{\tau} < 1
$$ {#eq-m11-wenckebach}

is the shortest cycle length with 1:1 conduction: 241 ms here, where the slope condition gives 0.93. Below
$\text{CL}_W$ conduction times lengthen beat by beat until one beat blocks, the node recovers, and the cycle repeats:
8:7 at 235 ms, 4:3 at 220 ms, 3:2 at 200 ms and 2:1 at 150 ms (lab part C). If the slope condition fails, the 1:1
state loses stability before $\text{CL}_W$.

::: {.demo #m11-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m11-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m11-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m11-d1-wenckebach.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m11-avnode and @eq-m11-wenckebach, iterated beat by beat; recovery time counted from the last conducted
  beat. Tested against `epml.epstudy`.
- Parameters: $\text{NCT}_{\min}$ = 57 ms, $\text{NCT}_{\max}$ = 150 ms and $\text{ERP}_N$ = 91 ms from rabbit
  preparations [@reid2003]; $\tau$ = 100 ms is illustrative.
- What it ignores: dual nodal pathways, concealed conduction [@xu2006], autonomic tone, fatigue and human values.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- The AV node's recovery curve turns incremental pacing into Wenckebach periodicity.
- The Wenckebach point is the refractory period plus the longest conduction time, if the 1:1 state is stable.

### Entrainment and the post-pacing interval

Pacing slightly faster than a reentrant tachycardia sends an orthodromic wave into the circuit that resets it to the
pacing rate, while the antidromic wave collides with the previous beat; when pacing stops the tachycardia continues
[@waldo1997]. After the last stimulus, the paced wave travels a distance $d$ to the circuit, goes once around and
returns, so:

$$
\text{PPI} - \text{TCL} \approx \frac{2d}{\text{CV}}, \qquad \text{PPI} \approx \text{TCL} \text{ on the circuit}
$$ {#eq-m11-ppi}

In simulations, Stevenson and colleagues showed that the PPI equals the tachycardia cycle length at circuit sites and
always exceeds it at bystander sites, and that slowing in the circuit during pacing lengthens the PPI
[@stevenson1993]. In a Mitchell–Schaeffer ring with a dead-end branch, PPI − TCL was 12 ms on the circuit, 83 ms at
10 mm and 148 ms at 20 mm, against 2d/CV = 72 and 148 ms; pacing 60 instead of 20 ms faster raised the on-circuit
value from 12 to 38 ms (lab parts D and E).

::: {.demo #m11-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m11-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m11-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m11-d2-ppi.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m11-ppi for a pacing site connected to the circuit by a path of length $d$ with uniform velocity.
  Tested against `epml.epstudy`.
- Parameters: distance and velocity are free choices for illustration.
- What it ignores: slowing during pacing (lab part E), decremental conduction, and the difference between stimulus
  and local activation at the pacing site.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- PPI minus TCL is the round trip from the pacing site to the circuit.
- Rate-related slowing adds to it, so pace only slightly faster than the tachycardia.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Catheter recording of His-bundle activity [@scherlag1969] is what separates AH from HV.
Recovery-curve studies in animal preparations describe the AV node's slow and fast pathways and concealed conduction
[@reid2003; @xu2006]. Entrainment was first described during pacing of atrial flutter and is used to identify mapping
sites within or outside a reentrant circuit [@waldo1997]. In 15 patients with ventricular tachycardia late after
myocardial infarction, radiofrequency current terminated tachycardia at 24 of 241 sites (10%); termination was more
likely where the PPI approximated the tachycardia cycle length, where entrainment showed concealed fusion, or where
the stimulus-to-QRS interval was more than 60 ms and less than 70% of the cycle length [@stevenson1993]. Mapping
systems display these timings; the physiology above is how they are read.

**What the evidence is.** A technique report [@scherlag1969], animal preparations [@reid2003; @xu2006], a review
[@waldo1997] and a combined simulation and clinical study [@stevenson1993].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **How was local activation timed on each deflection?** Intervals inherit that choice (@eq-m11-intervals).
- **At what pacing rate was the PPI measured?** Faster pacing lengthens it (@eq-m11-ppi).
- **Was capture of the circuit confirmed?** A PPI means nothing without entrainment.

## How experts think

When reading an EP study, ask:

1. **Where is the delay?** AH or HV (@eq-m11-intervals).
2. **Is AV conduction behaving like a node?** Decremental, with Wenckebach periodicity at fast
   rates (@eq-m11-wenckebach).
3. **What was the pacing protocol?** Train length, coupling intervals and pacing site all change the answer.
4. **Was the circuit entrained, and at what rate?** (@eq-m11-ppi)
5. **Does the PPI agree with the other criteria?** Concealed fusion alone can mislead [@stevenson1993].

One sentence to keep: **every number in an EP study is a timing, and every timing depends on how and where it was
measured.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Intervals (@eq-m11-intervals) | AH = $t_H - t_A$ (node); HV = $t_V - t_H$ (His–Purkinje) |
| AV nodal recovery (@eq-m11-avnode) | NCT falls from $\text{NCT}_{\max}$ at $\text{ERP}_N$ toward $\text{NCT}_{\min}$ |
| Wenckebach point (@eq-m11-wenckebach) | $\text{CL}_W = \text{ERP}_N + \text{NCT}_{\max}$ if $(\text{NCT}_{\max} - \text{NCT}_{\min})/\tau < 1$ |
| Post-pacing interval (@eq-m11-ppi) | $\text{PPI} - \text{TCL} \approx 2d/\text{CV}$; about 0 on the circuit |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Rabbit anterograde NCT 57–150 ms, nodal ERP 91 ms | @reid2003 |
| Odds ratios 4.6 (PPI ≈ TCL) and 3.4 (concealed fusion); 25% bystanders; 24 of 241 sites | @stevenson1993 |
| Recovery time constant 100 ms; interval times on the synthetic recording | illustrative |
| Conduction ratios, PPI values | our own code |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What do the AH and HV intervals measure?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

AH: conduction from the low atrium through the AV node to the His bundle. HV: conduction from the His bundle to the
earliest ventricular activation (@eq-m11-intervals).

</details>

**Q2. Why is the His deflection hard to time?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It is small and sits between large atrial and ventricular deflections; far-field signals and filtering shift the
steepest slope (@eq-m11-intervals; m04, m22).

</details>

**Q3. What is a recovery curve, and how is it measured?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Conduction time against the time since the last conducted beat, measured with premature beats after a steady train;
it ends at the effective refractory period (@eq-m11-avnode).

</details>

**Q4. Explain Wenckebach periodicity with the recovery curve.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Each beat's recovery time is the cycle length minus the previous conduction time; a longer conduction time shortens
the next recovery and lengthens the next conduction time, until recovery falls below the refractory period and a beat
blocks (@eq-m11-wenckebach).

</details>

**Q5. With $\text{ERP}_N$ = 91 ms and $\text{NCT}_{\max}$ = 150 ms, what is the Wenckebach point?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

241 ms, if the 1:1 state is stable there (@eq-m11-wenckebach).

</details>

**Q6. What is concealed conduction?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A blocked impulse that still enters the node and resets its excitability, so it affects the next beat without being
seen [@xu2006].

</details>

**Q7. Define entrainment.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Capture of a reentrant circuit by pacing slightly faster than the tachycardia, without terminating it; the
tachycardia continues when pacing stops [@waldo1997].

</details>

**Q8. Why does PPI − TCL estimate distance from the circuit?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The last paced wave travels to the circuit, around it and back, so the extra time is the round trip
$2d/\text{CV}$ (@eq-m11-ppi).

</details>

**Q9. The PPI is 40 ms longer than the TCL on a site you think is in the circuit. Possible reasons?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The site may be outside the circuit; or pacing was too fast and slowed conduction in the circuit; or the post-pacing
electrogram was mistimed (@eq-m11-ppi) [@stevenson1993].

</details>

**Q10. What is concealed fusion, and why is it not enough on its own?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Entrainment with no change in QRS morphology; it can also occur at bystander sites adjacent to the circuit, so the PPI
and stimulus-to-QRS interval are needed too [@stevenson1993].

</details>

**Q11. Why pace only slightly faster than the tachycardia when entraining?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Faster pacing slows conduction in the circuit and lengthens the PPI, and may terminate or change the
tachycardia (@eq-m11-ppi; lab part E).

</details>

**Q12. How would you test an automatic PPI calculator?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

On simulated circuits with known distances and velocities, at several pacing rates and noise levels, checking that
it times the local electrogram and not the stimulus artifact (@eq-m11-ppi).

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A at 40 ms, H at 125 ms, V at 170 ms. AH and HV?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

85 ms and 45 ms (@eq-m11-intervals).

</details>

**S2. With the model of this module, conduction time after a recovery time equal to $\text{ERP}_N$?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\text{NCT}_{\max}$ (@eq-m11-avnode).

</details>

**S3. Steady 1:1 conduction with NCT = 120 ms at CL 250 ms. Recovery time?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

130 ms (@eq-m11-wenckebach).

</details>

**S4. In a 4:3 Wenckebach pattern, how many atrial beats are blocked per cycle?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

One (@eq-m11-wenckebach).

</details>

**S5. A pacing site 15 mm from the circuit along a path conducting at 0.5 m/s. PPI − TCL?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

60 ms (@eq-m11-ppi).

</details>

**S6. PPI − TCL = 0 ms. Where is the pacing site, by this model?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

On the circuit (@eq-m11-ppi).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **The His-bundle recording.** Scherlag and colleagues show the first catheter recordings of His-bundle activity in
  man [@scherlag1969]. This module: intervals.
- **Entrainment at circuit and bystander sites.** Stevenson and colleagues diagram stimulus-to-QRS and post-pacing
  intervals in simulated circuits [@stevenson1993]. This module: entrainment.
- **Nodal recovery curves.** Reid and colleagues plot anterograde and retrograde recovery curves before and after
  pathway ablation [@reid2003]. This module: the AV nodal recovery curve.

## Further reading

- **Recording.** The His-bundle catheter technique [@scherlag1969].
- **The AV node.** Dual pathways and recovery [@reid2003]; concealed conduction [@xu2006].
- **Entrainment.** Atrial flutter [@waldo1997]; ventricular tachycardia circuits [@stevenson1993].
- **Related modules.** m04 (recording chain), m08 (refractoriness), m10 (reentry), m22 (annotation), m24 (activation
  maps).
